title: The valley of Hunayn
hookLine: the army, proud of its numbers, nearly breaks at Hunayn (9:25)

cards: A few weeks after Mecca opened, the Muslim army marched out to meet the tribe of Hawazin.

It was the biggest force they had ever gathered, around twelve thousand, and the early accounts say someone in the ranks said it out loud: we won't be beaten today for lack of numbers. You know the feeling.

The team is stacked, the spreadsheet looks great, and a little voice in your chest says: we can't lose. Before dawn they went down into a narrow valley called Hunayn. The enemy was already hidden in the slopes above them.

teach.b: The ambush broke over them in the half-dark: arrows from the slopes, the path too narrow to turn in. The great army ran. Camels bolted.
Men scattered back up the valley. The Qur'an doesn't hide this.

In the ninth surah it tells the believers, in Pickthall's words, that on the day of Hunayn, "ye exulted in your multitude but it availed you naught," and that the wide earth felt narrow to them, and they turned and fled.
That's an honest scripture, remembering its own community's worst morning. In the middle of the panic, the hadith collections say, the Prophet ﷺ did not run.

teach.h: HE STAYED, AND CALLED THEM BACK.
teach.b: He stayed on his white mule, with a handful of companions around him, and called out who he was: I am the Prophet, that is no lie.
His uncle al-'Abbas, who had a huge voice, shouted for the people to come back, and they came, turning their camels around.
Then, the surah says, God sent down His sakinah, a calm, a peace of reassurance, on the Prophet and the believers, and the battle turned. Muslim teachers draw a simple lesson from Hunayn.
The same people who had won at Badr when they were few almost lost when they were many. The difference wasn't the count; it was where their trust was resting.
Numbers can be good. They just can't be God. After the battle, the reports add, he was generous even with the defeated tribe, and many of Hawazin became Muslims.

how: Muslims recite 9:25–26 when warning against trusting in numbers or wealth, and the calm, sakinah, sent down at Hunayn is a word many use for the peace they ask God for in hard moments.

o: a calm from God that steadies a frightened heart
a quiet place set apart for prayer and rest
the courage to charge without any fear of death

games.q: what happened at Hunayn — tap the pairs.
p: shouted for the people to return

s: the Qur'an only tells of the Muslims' victories
at Hunayn it says they exulted in their numbers, it availed them naught, and they fled.
the Prophet ﷺ stayed when most ran
the hadith say he stayed on his mule with a few companions and called out who he was.
at Badr they were few; at Hunayn they were many
teachers use the pair: the count was not what decided it.

games.q: you're in the biggest army Medina has ever sent out. arrows come out of the dark and everyone around you is running. what does the Prophet ﷺ do?
o: he stays on his mule and calls the people back.
he orders a retreat to regroup at Mecca.
games.why: he stayed, calling I am the Prophet, that is no lie, and al-'Abbas's great voice brought them back. then the sakinah came down.

practice: Think of a number you lean on: followers, savings, years of experience, likes on a post, steps, grades.
Notice how it feels to think about it, a little taller maybe, then imagine it at zero for a moment and notice what's still there.
If you pray, you can place your trust back where Muslims say it belongs, with God; if you don't, just rest in whatever is left when the number is gone.

wordCard.voice: Sakinah, the calm sent down to the ones who stood, when the biggest army nearly broke in the valley of Hunayn.

orig.note: Arabic: calm, tranquility, the peace sent down on the believers at Hunayn (9:26).

carryVoice: Your line: numbers didn't help. The calm came to the ones who stood. Day two hundred eighty-one.

sources.q: ye exulted in your multitude but it availed you naught
